To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

biomarkers of normal tissue effects of radiation therapy are of potential interest, that dose-volume effects are of importance, that the search for biomarkers is a long-term effort, that it is important to adjust for dose-volume effects, and that it is important not to overinterpret the results of studies with small sample sizes.

(1) the dose-volume effect in the development of normal tissue toxicity is important to consider in biomarker studies, (2) the search for normal-tissue biomarkers is a promising field of research, and (3) the use of biomarkers for normal tissue toxicity of radiotherapy is still far from being a clinical reality, and further research is needed to identify the most promising biomarkers and to establish their clinical utility.

(a) radiation dose distribution is an important confounder in normal tissue biomarkers studies; and (b) the search for normal-tissue radiation biomarkers should focus on dose-volume effects and on dose-volume effects that are not yet known to be associated with specific radiation-induced normal tissue effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of biomarkers for predicting and monitoring normal tissue toxicity.
the development of biomarkers for normal tissue effects of radiation therapy, and the use of these biomarkers to predict, monitor and assess the efficacy of new radiation therapy techniques.
the development of novel molecular biomarkers for radiation side effects and the use of these markers in the design of new clinical trials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
biomarkers are a promising tool in normal tissue research, but that the search for clinically useful biomarkers is still in its infancy.
biomarkers have been identified and validated in animal models of normal tissue injury and in some human clinical settings.

there are currently no biomarkers or surrogate endpoints for radiation therapy side effects that have been validated in a clinical setting and that have been shown to be useful for clinical decision making.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

biomarkers for normal tissue effects of radiation therapy have been identified and are being studied in the context of radiation dose distributions, but that the clinical utility of these biomarkers remains to be established.
the search for biomarkers for normal tissue effects of radiation therapy is in its infancy and requires more basic research to identify and characterize potential biomarker candidates.
biomarkers and surrogate endpoints are promising for predicting and monitoring radiation side effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is an urgent need to develop a better understanding of the molecular and cellular basis of radiation-induced normal tissue damage, and to identify biomarkers that are sensitive to radiation and that can be measured in a clinically relevant manner.
the dose-volume effect is a key consideration in the development and interpretation of biomarkers of normal tissue response to radiation therapy.
biomarkers of normal tissue effects of radiation therapy should not only reflect molecular events but also take into account the radiation dose distribution in the normal tissues.
